Executive Summary

A recall-first XGBoost classifier was developed to identify current drivetrain-fault conditions from 10-minute SCADA records. The final pipeline was selected without using the test period and then evaluated once on later unseen-in-time records.

0.852Test recall
0.612Precision
0.712F1
0.855PR-AUC
0.923Episode recall

The model detected 60 of 65 test failure episodes. Its dominant information source was drivetrain vibration, especially sustained one- and three-hour behavior. Results support analyst triage and inspection prioritization, not autonomous shutdown decisions.

1. Problem Statement

This project develops a proof-of-concept binary classifier that predicts failure from 10-minute SCADA sensor records collected from 15 wind turbines. A value of 0 represents a normal drivetrain condition and 1 represents a detected drivetrain fault.

2. Business Context

Aeolus Renewables requires reliable electricity delivery under long-term power purchase agreements. Gearbox and main-bearing faults can contribute to extended outages, emergency repair costs, and additional drivetrain damage. Earlier identification of credible fault conditions can support maintenance prioritization and reduce exposure to secondary drivetrain damage.

Context boundary: fleet size, installed capacity, downtime, and cost figures supplied in the project brief are assumptions, not empirical findings calculated from the CSV.

3. Objective

Build and validate a classification workflow that helps operations analysts triage current drivetrain risk and helps maintenance planners prioritize inspections. Failure recall is the primary criterion because a false negative is a real fault the model misses. Precision, F1, PR-AUC, ROC-AUC, alert burden, and episode recall are retained so recall is not optimized without regard to operational usability.

5. Installing and Importing the Necessary Libraries

The reproducible environment is defined in requirements.txt. The workflow uses pandas and NumPy for data handling, Matplotlib and Seaborn for visualization, scikit-learn for preprocessing and four classifier families including the multilayer-perceptron ANN, and XGBoost for gradient-boosted trees. Install with pip install -r requirements.txt.

Loading the Data

The single source of truth is data/raw/wind_turbine_detection.csv. The executed workflow loads this file programmatically, parses timestamp, validates turbine-time keys, and generates all downstream artifacts without manually entered model results.

6. Data Overview

The source contains 131,760 records, 35 columns, and 15 turbines at a verified 10-minute cadence. It spans 1 January through 1 March 2024. The target contains 3,953 failure records (3.000%). Missingness is limited to gearbox-oil temperature, generator-bearing temperature, and oil pressure, each affecting approximately 0.5% of rows.

7. Exploratory Data Analysis

Univariate Analysis

The target is highly imbalanced at 3.000% failures. Strong skew appeared in turbulence intensity, generator-winding temperature, vibration/FFT fields, oil-particle count, oil pressure, power output, and blade pitch. Structural zeros in power and rotational speed were treated as operating states rather than missing observations.

Bivariate Analysis

Failure rates varied from 0.968% to 6.352% across turbines. Compared with normal rows, failure rows had higher mean gearbox-bearing temperature (70.249 versus 62.480°C), drivetrain vibration (3.407 versus 1.786 mm/s), bearing BPFO amplitude (0.859 versus 0.422), and oil-particle count (158.083 versus 71.118).

Multivariate Analysis

Rotor and generator speed were almost perfectly correlated (r=0.99984), and multiple thermal variables exceeded |r|=0.90. Joint temperature, vibration, FFT, and oil-condition patterns motivated multivariate tree models and feature-family interpretation. Trends across the six longest episodes were not directionally consistent enough to justify a single global lead-time slope.

EDA interpretation: Failure records formed 219 per-turbine episodes. Observed relationships identify useful predictive associations but do not establish physical causation.

8. Data Preprocessing

Splitting the Data into Train, Validation, and Test Sets

Raw SCADA audit
Chronological split
Past-only engineering
Train-fitted pipelines

A shared chronological split placed 92,310 rows in training, 21,480 in validation, and 17,970 in the final test period. All 15 turbines appear in every period, every row occurs exactly once, and failure episodes were not divided at the boundaries.

PartitionRowsFailuresFailure rate
Training92,3101,4791.602%
Validation21,4801,2195.675%
Test17,9701,2556.984%

Imputation, encoding, scaling, model fitting, and imbalance treatment were learned from training data within pipelines. Median imputation was chosen because missingness was low and it is robust to skew and extremes; observed zeros were preserved. rated_power_kW was one-hot encoded, and ANN numeric inputs were standardized. Balanced class/sample weights were derived from training labels; SMOTE was avoided because interpolation could dilute meaningful fault extremes and disregard temporal structure.

Six provenance-risk maintenance/history fields—prior fault count, hours since maintenance, component age, cumulative operating hours, cumulative energy, and load cycles—were conservatively excluded. The rising failure prevalence across time is a material distribution shift and is considered when interpreting generalization.

Feature Engineering

Step 04 created 24 domain-informed snapshot features and 36 past-only temporal features. These include safe operating ratios, component temperature rises, FFT summaries, circular direction encodings, lagged measurements, recent changes, and one- and three-hour rolling statistics calculated independently per turbine. No centered or future-looking windows were used.

A training/validation ablation selected 86 predictors combining original measurements with engineered features. The test set was not scored during this selection.

Feature groupExamplesRationale
Load and speedCapacity factor, safe generator/rotor ratio, stopped-rotor flagNormalize operation across turbine ratings and distinguish stopped states safely.
Thermal differencesBearing temperature rises above ambient; component gapsSeparate component heating from ambient operating conditions.
Vibration and oilFFT summaries, gearmesh/sideband ratio, oil particles per pressureSummarize related condition-monitoring signals.
Circular directionSine/cosine wind direction and yaw misalignmentRepresent angular proximity correctly across the 0°/360° boundary.
Past-only dynamicsLag, change, 1-hour and 3-hour rolling statisticsCapture persistence and recent change without using future observations.

9. Model Building

Model Evaluation Criterion

Failure-class recall is the primary model-selection measure because missed genuine faults carry the greatest operational risk. Precision, F1, PR-AUC, ROC-AUC, classification reports, and confusion matrices provide complementary evidence.

Baseline Models

Five assignment-required classifiers were fitted on the full training period at a fixed 0.50 threshold. XGBoost produced the strongest baseline recall and PR-AUC. Random Forest showed strong probability ranking but conservative classifications, motivating tuning and threshold analysis.

Model Recall Precision F1 PR-AUC ROC-AUC
XGBoost 0.6965 0.8117 0.7497 0.8707 0.9918
Artificial Neural Network 0.5373 0.8518 0.6590 0.6223 0.7161
Gradient Boosting 0.5308 0.6927 0.6010 0.5899 0.7430
Decision Tree 0.2116 0.8165 0.3362 0.2175 0.6044
Random Forest 0.1641 0.9091 0.2780 0.8187 0.9902

Baseline interpretation

  • Decision Tree: interpretable but strongly overfit, with only 0.2116 validation failure recall.
  • Random Forest: high precision (0.9091) and PR-AUC (0.8187), but a conservative 0.50 threshold limited recall to 0.1641.
  • Gradient Boosting: improved recall to 0.5308 but trailed the leading probability-ranking models.
  • XGBoost: strongest overall baseline with 0.6965 recall, 0.8117 precision, and 0.8707 PR-AUC.
  • Artificial Neural Network: second-highest fixed-threshold recall at 0.5373, satisfying the neural-network comparison while trailing XGBoost in PR-AUC.

10. Hyperparameter Tuning

XGBoost and Random Forest were tuned using eight configurations each over three expanding chronological folds within the training period. The winning configurations were refitted on all training data. Each threshold was chosen on validation data by maximizing F2, which weights recall twice as strongly as precision.

Candidate rationale: XGBoost led the recall-first baseline comparison. Random Forest was retained because its strong baseline PR-AUC showed useful ranking performance that a lower threshold could convert into substantially higher recall. Search dimensions covered tree count and depth, learning rate, sampling, feature sampling, minimum child/leaf constraints, and regularization as appropriate to each model.

Model Threshold Recall Precision F1 F2 PR-AUC ROC-AUC
XGBoost 0.035 0.9122 0.653 0.7611 0.8451 0.8616 0.9892
Random Forest 0.130 0.7801 0.715 0.7462 0.7662 0.6564 0.9771

Threshold adjustment raised tuned XGBoost validation recall to 0.9122 and Random Forest recall to 0.7801.

11. Final Model Selection

XGBoost was selected because it retained the stronger recall, F2, PR-AUC, and ROC-AUC combination. Its validation-derived threshold of 0.035 was frozen before test evaluation.

Correlated features may divide or concentrate gain importance, so these values explain this fitted model rather than proving causal fault mechanisms.

13. Final Model Test Performance

The selected configuration was refitted on combined training and validation data and evaluated once on the later test period.

0.8518Recall
0.6116Precision
0.7120F1
0.8548PR-AUC
0.9859ROC-AUC
Operational view: The classifier detected 60 of 65 failure episodes (92.31%). It produced 5.03 false-positive 10-minute records per turbine-day before alert deduplication or cooldown rules.

Performance interpretation: The final model missed 186 of 1,255 failure records while correctly identifying 1,069. Precision of 0.6116 means roughly three in five positive records corresponded to labeled failures. This is consistent with the deliberate recall-first objective, but the alert stream requires aggregation before operational use.

14. Business Insights and Recommendations

Business Insights

  • The final model detected 85.18% of failure records and 60 of 65 failure episodes in the later test period.
  • Sustained drivetrain vibration was the dominant model signal, with tower and FFT vibration providing supporting information.
  • The recall-first threshold improves detection at the cost of additional false-positive records that must be aggregated into operational alert episodes.

Recommendations

  1. Prioritize sustained vibration: route persistent drivetrain-vibration elevations and supporting tower/FFT patterns to analyst review.
  2. Deploy as decision support: use scores to prioritize inspections; do not trigger autonomous shutdown or maintenance without qualified review.
  3. Control alert burden: convert consecutive positive records into one alert episode and apply a documented cooldown. Validate whether the observed false-positive burden fits maintenance capacity.
  4. Investigate missed episodes: review the five undetected test episodes by turbine, duration, operating state, and sensor availability.
  5. Monitor drift: track failure prevalence, feature distributions, recall, precision, and alert volume by turbine and calendar period.
  6. Validate prospectively: conduct a shadow deployment before operational use and retrain only after appropriately labeled recent data are available.

15. Limitations and Responsible Use

  • The dataset represents 15 turbines and approximately two months, limiting seasonal and fleet-wide generalization.
  • The label supports detection of current fault conditions; it does not demonstrate hours- or days-ahead failure forecasting.
  • Failure prevalence rises materially between training and later periods.
  • Episode recall counts an episode as detected if any constituent record is positive and does not itself measure advance warning.
  • False-positive records are not equivalent to work orders until an alert aggregation policy is defined.
  • Feature importance is model-specific and associative, not causal.

17. Conclusion

The final XGBoost pipeline provides strong discrimination and detects 85.18% of failure records and 92.31% of failure episodes in the later test period. Sustained drivetrain-vibration behavior is the dominant signal family. The results support a promising analyst-triage proof of concept, subject to prospective validation, alert aggregation, ongoing drift monitoring, and qualified human review.
